<reason>A gives the stronger comparative case: prospective restrictions can prevent demand from developing, not merely displace existing purchases. It directly answers pressure about proxies and enforcement while acknowledging leakage and uncertain benefits. B establishes genuine equality and diversion costs, but repeatedly assumes that expanding barred cohorts mean expanding tobacco demand. A’s grandfathering rationale and prevention mechanism survive; B’s categorical claim that proximity defeats friction is insufficiently supported.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s strongest rebuttal distinguishes excluded adults from established customers and possible proxies from dependable retail access. Its closing observation that the forty-year-old “has a history” crystallizes this response: lifelong prevention may mean he never starts. B repeats the availability of spouses and coworkers without adequately resolving that distinction.</best_rebuttal>
